transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in today?

My mind keeps getting stuck on the same worrying thoughts about what I might have forgotten or done wrong, and I can’t seem to shut them off even when I’m not at school. It's just making me feel so exhausted lately.

Do these thoughts feel like intrusive, unwanted obsessions that you try to neutralize with repeated actions or mental rituals, or are they more like general worries about many different things in your life?

They definitely feel like intrusive, looping "what-ifs" that I can't shut off, like constantly worrying I wrote the wrong date on school permission slips or forgot to give my dad his medicine. To try and quiet those thoughts, I feel forced to repeat things over and over, like checking his pill boxes or rewriting my lesson plans and emails multiple times.
When you do the checking or rewriting, do you feel driven to repeat them until they feel 'just right' or until your anxiety drops, even though you know it takes a lot of time?

Yes, I feel completely driven to keep doing them, sometimes spending ten or fifteen minutes checking pill boxes or rewriting emails past when I meant to stop. I feel like if I don't, something terrible will happen and it will be entirely my fault. It takes up so much of my time and just leaves me feeling exhausted.
Do you recognize these thoughts and repeated checking as excessive or unreasonable, even while you feel unable to stop them?

Yes, when I step back, I know it's excessive and it's completely taking over my evenings and free time. But in the moment, the anxiety is so intense and the fear of something bad happening to my parents or my students feels so real that I feel totally unable to stop.
Do you also have any other repetitive behaviors or mental rituals, like counting, washing, arranging, or silently repeating words, that you feel you have to do to reduce the anxiety?

No, I don't really do things like counting, washing, or arranging. Instead, my repetitive behaviors are more about rereading emails, rewriting lesson plans, and repeatedly checking my parents' calendars and pill boxes to make sure nothing bad happens.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has classic obsessive-compulsive symptoms: intrusive, unwanted, repetitive doubt/worry thoughts; recognized as excessive; and compulsive checking/rewriting/re-reading rituals performed to reduce anxiety and prevent feared harm. Symptoms are time-consuming, distressing, and impair functioning, which is most consistent with obsessive-compulsive disorder.
